title: How Mercenaries Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and modern role of mercenaries, starting with Cyrus the Younger's Greek 'Ten Thousand' around 401 BC and the Hundred Years War, where the Black Prince used mercenaries for chevauchée raids. They cover Swiss Guard pikemen, German Landsknechte, Hessians in the Revolutionary War, and the 1977 Geneva Protocol's criteria defining a mercenary versus a lawful combatant. The episode then discusses modern private military contractors, including Blackwater and the 2007 Baghdad shooting, Simon Mann and Executive Outcomes and the failed 2004 Equatorial Guinea coup, the French Foreign Legion, contractor pay and benefits, non-war contractor work, and the risks of hiring mercenaries such as the Almogavars turning on Byzantium. The episode closes with listener mail about a near-death experience and a sign-off.
topics: How Stuff Works listener mail near death experience

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode, joking about Chuck arriving late and the topic of mercenaries, and Josh introduces the basic idea that mercenaries fight for money rather than ideology.

segments.title: Origins: Cyrus the Younger and the Ten Thousand
segments.summary: The earliest known account of mercenaries is Cyrus the Younger hiring the Ten Thousand, a Greek mercenary army, around 401 BC to seize the Persian throne. The hosts mention the movie 300 and its training.

segments.title: Hundred Years War and the Black Prince
segments.summary: Mercenaries were used in the Hundred Years War between England and France, where private armies were paid. Edward of Woodstock, the Black Prince, used mercenaries for chevauchee raids that burned, pillaged and looted. Use of mercenaries declined afterward.

segments.title: Famous historical mercenaries
segments.summary: The Swiss Guard, known as masters of the pike, and German mercenaries who used pikes and guns, were sought after for their combined weapons. Hessians fought in the Revolutionary War, with the hosts noting one was linked to the Headless Horseman legend.

segments.title: World War II and the 1977 Geneva Protocol definition
segments.summary: After standing armies became popular, mercenaries faded until World War II. Volunteers from other countries fought for Germany. The 1977 Geneva Protocol I defines a mercenary: specially recruited, not a member of the recruiting state's armed forces, actively engaged in hostilities, motivated by private gain, and paid substantially more than ordinary forces.

segments.title: Lawful combatants and Blackwater
segments.summary: The Geneva Conventions define lawful combatants, who are protected as prisoners of war, while mercenaries are outside that protection and can be tried for murder. The hosts discuss Blackwater and the 2007 Baghdad shooting that killed civilians, and the US not signing a UN convention against mercenaries.

segments.title: Why the US uses contractors and Africa mercenary history
segments.summary: Contractors handle security duties because soldiers are spread thin. The hosts cite estimates of over 180,000 contractors in Iraq and about $100 billion spent. They then discuss Simon Mann, Executive Outcomes, and the failed 2004 plot against the government of Equatorial Guinea, which allegedly involved Mark Thatcher.

segments.title: French Foreign Legion
segments.summary: The French Foreign Legion, established in 1831, recruits foreigners who sign five-year contracts and can gain French citizenship. Recruits go through selection and fifteen weeks of basic training, receive the white cape blanc, and serve in regiments worldwide. More than 35,000 legionnaires have died in combat since 1831.

segments.title: Contractor pay, non-combat work, and risks of hiring mercenaries
segments.summary: Contractors earn roughly $600 to $1,000 a day but pay their own benefits and taxes. They also do non-combat work such as anti-poaching training in the Congo, corporate security, and counter-drug operations. The hosts note the risk of disloyalty, citing the Almogavars who turned on the Byzantines.

segments.title: Listener mail: near-death experience
segments.summary: A listener from Boston shares her mother's account of a near-death experience at age three, in which a girl on a yellow school bus told her she was too young to board. The hosts thank listeners for their stories.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh points listeners to HowStuffWorks for more on mercenaries and invites emails about soldier-of-fortune or line cook stories.
